steps.body: The sieve finds every prime in a range by elimination: cross out the multiples of 2, then 3, then 5, and whatever survives is prime.
steps.narration: The sieve finds every prime in a range by elimination: cross out the multiples of 2, then 3, then 5, and whatever survives is prime.

widget.prompt: Run the multiples-of-3 pass: count by 3s from 0 and watch which numbers get crossed out.

commonLandings.feedback: Five hops reach 15; the sixth landing is the one being tested.
Seven hops overshoot — the sixth multiple of 3 is 18.

widget.missFeedback: Each hop covers 3, so six of them reach 18.
widget.successFeedback: 18 — and every landing on the way (3, 6, 9, 12, 15) is crossed out as a multiple of 3.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — each hop covers 3, so six of them reach 18.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — six hops of 3 stop exactly on 18.

predict.prompt: After crossing out multiples of 2, is a separate pass for 4 needed?
predict.reveal: Every multiple of 4 is also a multiple of 2, so the first pass already removed them all.

cml.actionGoal: Build the arrangements a number allows, and read the rule that generates the next term for g4pf sieve.
invariants: A factor pair is a rectangle a number can build and a multiple is a landing a count reaches, so every claim about g4pf sieve can be settled by construction rather than recall.
misconceptions: Reading an additive gap as a multiplier, stopping a factor search before the pairs repeat, or treating 1 as prime.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Which numbers would make this rectangle impossible to build with whole-number sides?

widget.prompt: In a sieve you cross out multiples of 2, then 3, then 5. Why is 4 never used as a crossing-out number?

options.label: Every multiple of 4 is even
options.feedback: Correct — 4 is itself composite, so its multiples are also multiples of its factor 2 and are gone already.

options.label: Because 4 has no multiples
options.feedback: 4 has infinitely many multiples; the point is they were already removed by an earlier pass.

options.label: Because 4 is prime
options.feedback: 4 is composite — it is 2 × 2 — which is exactly why it is skipped as a sieve number.

options.label: Because 4 is too small to matter
options.feedback: Size is not the reason; 5 is used and 4 is not, because only PRIMES add new crossings.

steps.body: Run a different sieve pass and explain the equally spaced composite landings it removes.

widget.prompt: Run the multiples-of-5 pass: count by 5s from 0 through 25.

commonLandings.feedback: 20 is four hops of 5. Continue one more equal hop to reach 25.

widget.missFeedback: The fifth equal hop of 5 lands on 25; those non-prime multiples are removed by this sieve pass.
widget.successFeedback: 25 — the fifth multiple of 5. It is crossed out because it has factors besides 1 and itself.

widget.prompt: The 3-pass crosses out 6, 9, 12, 15, and so on. Which is the smallest number it crosses out that the 2-pass had NOT already removed?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is even, so the 2-pass had already crossed it out — the 3-pass adds nothing new there.
3 is the sieve number itself and survives as a prime; the pass crosses out its MULTIPLES beyond it.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Go through the 3-pass landings in order — 6, 9, 12 — and ask of each: is it even?
widget.successFeedback: Correct — 9. Every earlier landing of the 3-pass is even and was already gone.

widget.prompt: After the 2-, 3-, and 5-passes of a sieve, why can 7 remain uncrossed?

options.label: No earlier sieve number divides 7 exactly
options.feedback: Correct — 7 is not a multiple of 2, 3, or 5, so those composite-removing passes do not cross it out.

options.label: Every odd number remains
options.feedback: Odd composite numbers such as 9 and 15 are crossed out by the 3- and 5-passes.

options.label: 7 is a multiple of 5
options.feedback: 7 ÷ 5 leaves a remainder, so 7 is not a multiple of 5.

options.label: The sieve skips all numbers below 10
options.feedback: The sieve starts with small numbers; it crosses out 4, 6, 8, and 9 before reaching 10.

options.feedback: Correct — 11 has no factors besides 1 and itself, so the only rectangle it builds is 1 by 11.

options.label: Composite
options.feedback: 11 has no factor pair other than 1 and 11, so it cannot be composed of smaller whole-number sides.
